faq.a: Flukes have not yet reached the bile ducts to lay eggs; ova appear 8‑12 weeks after infection.
faq.q: Why is stool microscopy often negative early?

faq.a: Yes, migrating larvae can produce necrotic tracks that mimic abscesses on imaging.
Data are limited; use only if benefits outweigh risks, as untreated disease can be fatal.

exam: A 28‑year‑old farmer presents with RUQ pain, fever, and eosinophilia after eating raw watercress – what is your next diagnostic step? — Order serum Fasciola IgG ELISA; imaging if ELISA unavailable.

How does fascioliasis differ from clonorchiasis in presentation and epidemiology? — Fascioliasis has an acute hepatic migration phase and is linked to freshwater plants; clonorchiasis is chronic, linked to raw fish, and endemic in East Asia.

A patient with confirmed fascioliasis develops cholangitis – which antibiotic regimen is appropriate and why? — Start a third‑generation cephalosporin (e.g., ceftriaxone) to cover Gram‑negative biliary pathogens; add metronidazole if anaerobes suspected.
Why is triclabendazole preferred over praziquantel for fascioliasis? — Triclabendazole is active against both immature and adult flukes; praziquantel has poor efficacy against Fasciola species.
What are the key features on ultrasound that suggest acute fascioliasis? — Multiple hypoechoic, ill‑defined lesions in the hepatic parenchyma representing migrating larvae.

Explain why eosinophilia may be absent in chronic fascioliasis and how you would still confirm the diagnosis. — Chronic infection may have low parasite activity; rely on imaging of biliary dilatation and repeat serology or stool microscopy after 12 weeks.

What immediate actions are needed for a fascioliasis patient presenting with hepatic encephalopathy? — Stabilize airway, treat hyperammonemia, start broad‑spectrum antibiotics for possible cholangitis, and arrange urgent referral for definitive antiparasitic therapy.
ai.title: Fascioliasis
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Fascioliasis is a trematode infection of the liver and biliary tree caused by Fasciola hepatica or Fasciola gigantica. It presents with acute hepatic inflammation followed by chronic biliary obstruction, especially in low‑resource tropical settings.

b: Endemic in East Africa, South America, and parts of Asia
Two clinical phases: acute (hepatic) and chronic (biliary)
sections.p: Fascioliasis is acquired by ingesting metacercariae on aquatic plants or contaminated water. The parasites migrate through the intestinal wall, peritoneum, and liver parenchyma before residing in the bile ducts.

b: Eosinophil count >500 µL strongly suggests acute phase
Serum IgG ELISA is most sensitive in early disease
Ultrasound shows hypoechoic lesions or biliary dilatation
sections.p: Diagnosis relies on a combination of exposure history, eosinophilia, liver imaging, and serology; stool microscopy is often negative early.

t.b: Confirms chronic infection; ova appear 8‑12 weeks after exposure; negative early does not rule out disease
Detects antibodies in acute phase; positive supports diagnosis when ova absent
Identifies migratory hepatic lesions in acute phase and biliary dilatation or flukes in chronic phase
Eosinophilia (>500 µL) indicates parasitic invasion; absence does not exclude chronic disease

b: Acute phase: fever, RUQ pain, hepatomegaly, eosinophilia
Chronic phase: intermittent jaundice, pruritus, cholangitis
sections.p: Patients may present with right‑upper‑quadrant pain, fever, jaundice, and marked eosinophilia. Complications include biliary obstruction, cholangitis, secondary bacterial infection, and hepatic fibrosis.

b: Ask about consumption of raw watercress or other aquatic greens
Differentiate fascioliasis from other eosinophilic liver diseases (e.g., schistosomiasis, visceral larva migrans)
Know that triclabendazole is drug of choice
sections.p: Examiners test ability to link exposure, eosinophilia, and imaging; to choose appropriate therapy; and to recognise pitfalls when ova are absent.

b: Triclabendazole targets adult flukes and immature stages; avoids nitroimidazoles which are ineffective
If triclabendazole unavailable, consider bithionol with caution (risk of hemolysis in G6PD deficiency)
Supportive: analgesia, antipyretics, hydration, and vitamin A in children
Schistosomiasis mansoni – periportal fibrosis, no acute hepatic migration
Visceral larva migrans (Toxocara) – systemic eosinophilia without biliary obstruction
Clonorchis sinensis – endemic in East Asia, presents with chronic cholangitis but no acute hepatic phase
sections.p: Other hepatic eosinophilic conditions and biliary parasites.

b: Relying solely on ova detection misses up to 70 % of acute cases
Serology may remain positive after successful treatment; correlate with clinical response
sections.p: Negative stool microscopy early in disease may falsely reassure; eosinophilia can be absent in chronic phase.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe jaundice with mental status change (possible hepatic encephalopathy)
High‑grade fever and right‑upper‑quadrant tenderness suggesting cholangitis
